skill.name: Sensory imagery: which sense, what picture
skill.why: Words for your senses put you right inside the scene.
skill.how: Ask: could I see, hear, smell, taste or touch this? Then picture it.

beats.say: Good writing makes you feel like you're really there.

beats.show: A **bright orange** crab waved one **huge white claw**.
Rain **drummed** on the tin roof all night.

beats.say: Others help you smell, taste or touch.
Words for the senses are called sensory imagery. Ask: which sense?

encounters.frame: Mo is cooking a barbecue on the jetty. A Whiskrel has crept up to watch.
encounters.text: It was Saturday night on the jetty. Mo was in charge of the barbecue. He wore a chef's hat that was much too big. First he cooked the sausages. Then he threw a pile of onions onto the hot plate. The onions hissed and crackled. The crew lined up with their plates. Gus wanted six sausages. Tully wanted extra sauce. The Whiskrel wanted everything, but it got one onion.
encounters.prompt: Read this line: 'The onions hissed and crackled.' Which sense does it wake up?
encounters.success: Hearing. A hiss and a crackle are noises. You hear them with your ears.

options.reason: Nobody is eating the onions yet. Hissing and crackling are noises.
You can't see a hiss. Hissing and crackling are sounds.

It was only Mo, holding a torch and a sausage.

encounters.frame: Zed is telling the crew about the rocket launch he saw on a school trip.
encounters.text: Our class went to watch a rocket launch. We stood far away behind a fence. A voice counted down from ten. At zero, the rocket lifted off. We felt the ground shake under our feet. The rocket went up and up. Soon it was just a tiny dot. Then it was gone. Our teacher said it was going all the way to space.

encounters.success: Touch. They felt the ground shake through their feet. That's something your body feels.

encounters.frame: Zed is learning guitar for Mangrove Music Night. He wrote about his first lesson.
encounters.text: My first guitar lesson was on Tuesday after school. The teacher, Mr Okafor, lent me an old guitar with a crack in the back. He showed me how to hold it and how to press down on the strings. My first chord sounded like a cat sitting on a keyboard. By the end of the hour, I could play three chords and half a song. My fingertips stung from pressing the hard steel strings. Mr Okafor said that was normal, and that my fingers would toughen up in a few weeks. At home, I played the half-song for Mum fourteen times. She said it was lovely the first time.

encounters.success: Touch. Stinging fingertips and hard strings are things Zed feels with his skin.

options.reason: The guitar makes sounds, but this line is about how the strings feel on his fingers.
You can't see a sting. Zed feels it in his fingertips.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote about snorkelling in the channel past the mangroves.
encounters.text: We anchored the boat at the mouth of the channel and jumped in. The water was clear and green. Fish flashed silver and blue around my legs. My wetsuit squeezed me like a sausage skin. Out past the rocks, the waves boomed against the reef. A gull screeched overhead, hoping we had chips. Back on the boat, the air smelled of seaweed and sunscreen. My hands were wrinkly for an hour. Gus said he saw a shark, but it was a log. The log did look a bit like a shark.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote about switching on his new robot for the first time. The Whiskrel hid under the bench.
encounters.text: At midnight, I flipped the switch. For a moment, nothing happened. Then a fan inside the robot began to whirr. Something deep in its chest went clunk, clunk, clunk. Its motors buzzed and its joints squeaked as it slowly stood up. A tiny speaker beeped three times. Then came a long hiss, like air out of a tyre. The robot took one step forward and its foot landed with a heavy thud. A second thud followed. Then it stopped, gave one sad beep and switched itself off. I think it needs more snot-glue.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing a funny story about Mo's cabin. The Whiskrel refuses to go in.
encounters.text: Nobody wanted to go into Mo's cabin. Even the Whiskrel, which happily rolls in mangrove mud, stopped at the door and backed away. Indi decided to put the cabin in her story. She wanted the reader to know it without even looking. She wanted them to wrinkle their noses as they read. She had a pile of old socks to work with, and some toast Mo had burnt three days ago. Mo said his cabin was 'lived in'. Tully said it was a health hazard, and Wren made everyone wash their hands after going near the door. Indi chewed her pencil and thought about which words to use.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote about the wettest footy game of the season for the island newsletter.
encounters.text: It had been raining since breakfast, and by the time the Reef Rays ran out for the second half, the oval was more like a swamp. Puddles lay across the centre square, and every pack of players ended in a heap of mud. Our coach told us to keep the ball low and use our feet. Early in the third quarter, Jada marked the ball in the pocket and lined up for goal. She had kicked that shot a hundred times at training. This time, though, the leather ball was slick with rain and slipped through her fingers as she dropped it onto her boot. It skidded off the side of her foot and rolled out of bounds. The crowd groaned. Jada stood with her hands on her knees for a moment, then jogged back into position. Ten minutes later, she kicked the goal that won us the game, and she says she has never been so happy to be soaking wet.
encounters.prompt: Read this line: 'The leather ball was slick with rain and slipped through her fingers.' Which sense does it wake up most?
encounters.success: Touch. A slippery ball sliding through her fingers is something Jada feels with her hands.

options.reason: You might picture the rain, but the line is about how the wet ball feels in her hands.
The line has no sounds in it. It's about a slippery ball in her fingers.

encounters.frame: A space station diary has been pinned to the Mirage Mangroves school library wall.
encounters.text: Day 40 on the station. I'm writing this while floating upside down, which is the only way I can reach my notebook. Out of the big round window, Earth hangs below us, a swirl of blue and white. Everything on board is strapped down, even the pens. The station hums day and night, a low drone that I don't even notice any more. This morning, three alarms beeped in a row, and my heart nearly stopped, but it was only the reminder for our exercise session. For lunch I had freeze-dried curry, which tasted like salty cardboard. I squeezed it out of a pouch and chased the floating blobs around with a spoon. Before bed I hold the metal handrail to pull myself into my sleeping bag, and it's icy against my palm. I miss rain. I miss toast. Most of all, I miss being able to put something down without it floating away.

encounters.frame: Mo wrote about the Mirage Mangroves night market for the island newsletter.
encounters.text: Every Thursday, as soon as the sun goes down, the car park beside the ferry turns into the night market. Strings of coloured lanterns sway between the stalls, and the crowd is so thick that you have to shuffle sideways to get anywhere. At one end, a band thumps away on a little stage while kids dance in front of it. Stallholders shout out their prices over the music. Smoke curls up from the satay grill, carrying the smell of peanut sauce and charcoal across the whole car park. Next door, a woman flips roti on a hot plate, and the smell of butter and sugar makes everyone in the queue lean forward. I had a bag of hot doughnuts, so fresh they burnt my fingers, and a mango smoothie so thick I had to eat it with a spoon. By nine o'clock, my ears were ringing, my shirt smelled like satay, and I was already planning next Thursday.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote notes on the flying fox camp. Zed summed them up, but got one word wrong.
encounters.text: Field notes, Tuesday. Today the ranger took me to the flying fox camp in the tall mangroves near the creek. You can find the camp long before you see it, because of the sour, musty stink that hangs over the whole creek. Hundreds of flying foxes hang upside down from the branches, wrapped in their wings like little umbrellas. As we walked closer, the camp woke up, and their wings rustled like paper. The ranger was caring for a young one that had hurt its wing on a fence. She let me hold it in a towel. When I touched its wing with one fingertip, it was warm and leathery, like a soft old glove. It looked up at me with big brown eyes and licked the juice off my finger. We gave it some mashed pear and put it back in its cage to rest. The ranger thinks it will be ready to fly again in about three weeks.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing the opening scene for his own game, Mangrove Dungeon. The Whiskrel is the hero.
encounters.text: Zed had been designing his game for weeks. The hero was a brave little Whiskrel, and the first level was a dungeon under the roots of an ancient mangrove. He had drawn the map, named every room and chosen the music. Now he was writing the words that would pop up on screen at the very start. The trouble was that the first room was pitch black. The player wouldn't be able to see a thing until they found a torch. Zed wanted the player to know where they were anyway, just from what they could hear. He wanted them to listen hard and feel a bit nervous before they took their first step. His first try said, 'You are in a dungeon. It is dark.' Tully read it over his shoulder and said it was about as scary as a sock drawer. He crossed out his first try, chewed his pen and started again.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote about her first night aboard the Soggy Biscuit. The Whiskrel slept through all of it.
encounters.text:
My first night aboard the Soggy Biscuit was not what I had imagined. I had pictured myself drifting off to sleep under the stars, rocked gently by the tide, dreaming about the Creatures we would rescue. Instead, Tully pointed me to a narrow bunk below deck, squeezed between a cupboard full of tins and a pile of Gus's experiments, and switched off the only light.

I lay there in the pitch dark with my eyes shut, trying not to think about what might be in the experiments. That was when the boat began to talk. The groan of the old hull timbers and the slap of loose rope against the mast kept me awake for hours. Somewhere near my feet, water gurgled through a pipe. Above me, footsteps creaked across the deck as someone on watch walked from one end to the other and back again. Every few minutes, Mo, in the next bunk, let out a snore like a small motorbike starting up.

At some point I must have fallen asleep, because the next thing I knew, sunlight was pouring through the porthole and Mo was offering me a fried egg on a slice of toast that was, somehow, also wet. I said yes. By the third night, I could sleep through anything.
encounters.prompt: Read this line: 'The groan of the old hull timbers and the slap of loose rope against the mast kept me awake for hours.' Which sense does it wake up?
encounters.success: Hearing. Wren is lying in the dark with her eyes shut, and a groan and a slap are sounds.

Nothing in the line has a smell. Groans and slaps are sounds that keep her awake.

encounters.frame: Wren sneaked into Maxx's Green Screen Swamp and wrote down everything she noticed.
encounters.text: Notes from inside Green Screen Swamp, 11.40 pm. The door was unlocked, which is typical of Maxx. Inside, it isn't a swamp at all. It's a huge shed, and almost every surface is painted the same flat, glowing green so that Maxx can add fake backgrounds later. Gold spotlights blaze down on a plastic waterfall that pours the same water round and round in a loop. As I creep past it, I can feel cold spray on the back of my neck. Fans whirr everywhere, and a generator in the corner thuds like a giant heartbeat. Somewhere above me, a robot camera gives a little buzz every few seconds. The air reeks of hot plastic and hairspray, which I think is mostly Maxx. A sour whiff of old fish food drifts out from behind the waterfall. Behind the waterfall, I found what we came for: rows of tiny cages stacked against the back wall. When I pressed my palms against the bars of the nearest one, they were cold and greasy, as if nobody had cleaned them in months. A Creature inside blinked at me. I took photos of everything, then crept out before the spotlights could swing my way.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote up a famous food critic's review of Mo's Mangrove Cafe. One word in her summary is wrong.
encounters.text:
MO'S MANGROVE CAFE: A REVIEW. I have eaten at restaurants on every island in the archipelago, but none of them prepared me for Mo's Mangrove Cafe, a wobbly wooden hut perched on the end of the jetty. I arrived just after sunset. Strings of fairy lights hung over the tables, and the menu was written in chalk on an old surfboard.

I ordered the house special, a mud crab curry. While I waited, I could hear it before I could see it: the curry spat and bubbled in a huge pot behind the counter, and every few seconds something went pop. When it arrived, the first spoonful tasted rich and nutty, then salty, then, strangely, a little bit sweet, as if somebody had stirred in a spoonful of jam. I asked Mo about this. He said it was 'a family secret', and then admitted that it was jam.

For dessert, I tried the sticky date pudding. The bowl was so hot that it warmed my hands right through, which was welcome, because the wind off the water was cold. I would not call the meal perfect, but I would call it unforgettable, and I am already planning to return, although perhaps not for the curry.

encounters.frame: Zed found this story in the Mirage Mangroves library. The Whiskrel read it from under a blanket.
encounters.text:
Nobody had been inside the old fishing shed at the end of the creek for years. From the outside, it looked like it might fall down if someone sneezed. The tin walls were orange with rust, the windows were boarded up, and a crooked sign on the door said KEEP OUT in faded red paint. Jas and her cousin Theo had dared each other all summer, and on the last night of the holidays, they finally squeezed through the gap in the door with one torch between them.

They had only taken five steps when the torch flickered and died. Theo shook it. Nothing. In the total darkness, the shed seemed to wake up. Something dripped steadily, plink, plink, plink, somewhere above their heads. The tin roof ticked and popped as it cooled. Behind them, the door creaked slowly shut. Then, from the far corner, came a scratching sound, followed by a soft, wet shuffle, as if something heavy was dragging itself across the floor towards them. Jas grabbed Theo's sleeve. Neither of them breathed.

Then Theo's phone lit up with a message from his mum, and in its blue glow they saw a very large, very startled pelican waddling across the floor towards them, dragging an old fishing net behind it. The pelican looked at them. They looked at the pelican. All three of them left the shed at the same time.

encounters.success: The torch has died, so Jas and Theo can't see. Sounds are all they have, which makes it scarier.

options.reason: The sounds are small: drips, ticks and a shuffle. They're scary because of the dark, not painful.

because the writer wants us to know the shed is about to fall
options.reason: Ticks and drips aren't signs of falling. The shed is just cooling and leaking in the dark.

options.reason: The passage never says they shut their eyes. The torch died, so it's totally dark.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote a review of the outdoor concert at the mangrove amphitheatre.
encounters.text:
The Mangrove Moonlight Concert has been running for twelve years, and this year it was the biggest yet, with more than a thousand people squeezed onto the grassy slope of the amphitheatre. The headline act was a five-piece band from the mainland called The Fiddler Crabs, and by the time they walked on stage, the crowd had been waiting for over an hour in the steamy evening heat.

The moment they started, purple and blue lights swept across the crowd, catching the raised arms and the bubbles drifting up from the front row. The drummer's sticks cracked against the snare like a whip, and the singer's voice soared over the top of it all. Halfway through the second song, a light rain began to fall, but nobody moved. Sweat ran down the back of my neck in the sticky heat. People stood on the hill singing every word. The smell of popcorn and wet grass drifted up from the stalls behind us.

The band played for nearly two hours and finished with an encore that had the whole hill jumping. Walking back to the ferry afterwards, my ears still buzzing and my shirt soaked through, I decided it was the best concert I have ever been to.
